interactions.summary: A student proposes that God has a plan for each person, but free will consists in choosing whether to follow that plan or resist it.
Jiang restates free will as the ability to deny God's call even though the deepest structure of the universe is reciprocal love between God and the soul.
A student presses the hardest case: if God knows Dante's persecutors will exile him, does that mean God planned their evil action too?
Another student interjects that the persecutors sin out of their own free will rather than by God's plan.
The questioner immediately pushes back that if their evil was not planned, God's foreknowledge still needs explaining.
Jiang narrows divine intention to the soul's return to God and says worldly events do not alter that larger teleology.
The student restates the objection more sharply, asking how a good God could both know and somehow authorize bad actors if they truly have free will.
Jiang responds that Dante's persecutors receive a worse fate than Dante, implying that prophecy does not excuse them or turn them into innocent instruments.

claims.claim: A student defines free will as the power to either follow or reject a divine plan that still exists for each person.
Jiang says the universe is structured by God's love calling the soul back to God, and free will names the capacity to deny that call and turn away.
A student frames the central objection to providence as the case of Dante's persecutors: if God foreknows their evil, it becomes difficult to separate foreknowledge from planning.
A student insists that the persecutors' wrongdoing comes from their own free will rather than from God's plan.
Jiang says God's plan is not about micromanaging worldly events but about drawing souls back to God, so earthly outcomes do not disturb the grand logic of return.
Jiang answers the moral objection by emphasizing that Dante's persecutors suffer a worse fate than Dante, so prophecy does not cancel moral judgment on their actions.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang compresses the cosmos into a love-structure: God calls the soul back, the soul desires return, and freedom appears precisely as the ability to refuse that pull.
signature_moments.source_phrase: you have the free will to deny god and turn away from god
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It gives the lecture its sharpest positive definition of free will, not as neutral option space but as resistance to a loving order.

signature_moments.moment: To save providence from the evil objection, Jiang shifts scale and says God does not really care about the local political event in itself compared with the larger return of souls.
signature_moments.source_phrase: god doesn't really care what happens here
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is a jarring formulation that reveals how radically Jiang subordinates history to teleology.

signature_moments.moment: The students force the abstract paradox into its ugliest form: would a good God script the bad actors who exile Dante and then damn them for the role?
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It keeps the packet from settling for easy compatibilism and preserves the real moral pressure in the room.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Here free will is defined as the ability to either cooperate with or resist the divine pull back toward God.
Jiang narrows the phrase to the soul's return to God rather than detailed control of every historical event.
Jiang uses comparative afterlife judgment to argue that persecutors remain responsible even if their actions fit a larger providential story.

chronology_notes.note: On 2026-06-17 Jiang answers the free-will/prophecy paradox by defining divine plan at the level of return to God and by preserving punishment for persecutors, rather than by denying either moral agency or providence outright.

uncertainty_notes.note: Jiang's formulation that God 'doesn't really care what happens here' is rhetorically stark and may be an overcompressed way of ranking earthly events below salvation rather than denying all historical concern.
